ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: As shown in the figure, several sufficiently long smooth straight tracks make different angles with the horizontal plane, and small balls are launched from point P along the respective tracks with initial velocities of different magnitudes. If each small ball happens to reach its own highest point within the same time, what relationship do the positions of the highest points of the small balls have?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, starting from point P at the lower left, there is a horizontal dashed line extending to the right indicating the horizontal plane; from point P several smooth straight tracks extend toward the upper right, they make different angles with the horizontal plane, and the tracks are sufficiently long. The small balls move upward along these tracks with different inclination angles respectively. Then reason: Let the common time used by all the small balls to reach their respective highest points from point P be T. Take P as the coordinate origin, horizontally to the right as the x-axis, and vertically upward as the y-axis. For a track making an angle θ with the horizontal plane, the magnitude of the acceleration of gravity along the track direction is g sinθ, and the direction is downward along the track, so the acceleration along the track is -g sinθ. When the small ball reaches the highest point, its velocity along the track is 0, therefore 0=v0-gT sinθ, that is, v0=gT sinθ. The displacement along the track to the highest point is s=v0T-1/2·g sinθ·T^2=1/2·gT^2 sinθ. Let a=1/2·gT^2, then s=a sinθ. The coordinates of this highest point are x=s cosθ=a sinθ cosθ, y=s sinθ=a sin^2θ. Eliminate θ: because x^2+y^2=s^2=a^2 sin^2θ, and y=a sin^2θ, so x^2+y^2=ay, that is, x^2+(y-a/2)^2=(a/2)^2. This is the equation of a fixed circle, independent of the track inclination angle θ. Therefore the highest points of all the small balls all fall on the same circumference.
